problem.title: Гена, возьми определитель
problem.statement:
Найдите сумму всех положительных значений \(a\), при которых матрица
\[
A=\bigl(\min(i,j)\cdot a^{|i-j|}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{2026}
\]
вырождена.
problem.solution:
Обозначим \(n=2026\).

Для \(i=n,n-1,\ldots,2\) заменим строку \(R_i\) на \(R_i-aR_{i-1}\). Исходная матрица
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1\cdot a^0&1\cdot a^1&1\cdot a^2&\cdots&1\cdot a^{n-1}\\
1\cdot a^1&2\cdot a^0&2\cdot a^1&\cdots&2\cdot a^{n-2}\\
1\cdot a^2&2\cdot a^1&3\cdot a^0&\cdots&3\cdot a^{n-3}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
1\cdot a^{n-1}&2\cdot a^{n-2}&3\cdot a^{n-3}&\cdots&n\cdot a^0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
переходит в верхнетреугольную матрицу
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1\cdot a^0&1\cdot a^1&1\cdot a^2&\cdots&1\cdot a^{n-1}\\
0&(2-a^2)\cdot a^0&(2-a^2)\cdot a^1&\cdots&(2-a^2)\cdot a^{n-2}\\
0&0&(3-2a^2)\cdot a^0&\cdots&(3-2a^2)\cdot a^{n-3}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&0&\cdots&(n-(n-1)a^2)\cdot a^0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

После этих преобразований определитель не поменялся, а матрица стала верхнетреугольной, поэтому
\[
\det A=\prod_{i=2}^{n}\bigl(i-(i-1)a^2\bigr).
\]
Отсюда
\[
a^2=\frac{i}{i-1}
\]
для некоторого \(i\in\{2,\ldots,n\}\). Следовательно, сумма всех положительных значений \(a\) равна
\[
\sum_{i=2}^{2026}\sqrt{\frac{i}{i-1}}\approx 2028.939215760406073.
\]

\[
A=\bigl(\min(i,j)\cdot a^{|i-j|}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{2026}
\]
вырождена.

results.answer:
The matrix \(A\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix with entries
\[
A_{ij} = \min(i,j) \cdot a^{|i-j|},
\]
where \(n = 2026\) and \(a > 0\). The goal is to determine all values of \(a > 0\) for which \(A\) is singular and to compute the sum of these values.

Let \(\rho = a > 0\). For an arbitrary vector \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top\), define the auxiliary quantities
\[
t_i = \sum_{j=i}^n \rho^{j-i} x_j, \quad i = 1, \dots, n
\]
(with the convention \(t_{n+1} = 0\)). These satisfy the backward recurrence
\[
t_i = x_i + \rho \, t_{i+1}, \quad i = 1, \dots, n-1,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
x_i = t_i - \rho \, t_{i+1}, \quad i = 1, \dots, n-1, \qquad x_n = t_n.
\]
Conversely, for any choice of the sequence \((t_1, \dots, t_n)\), the vector \(x\) defined by the preceding formulae produces exactly those \(t_i\).

Denote \(s = A x\), so that the \(i\)-th component is
\[
s_i = \sum_{j=1}^i j \, \rho^{i-j} x_j + i \sum_{j=i+1}^n \rho^{j-i} x_j.
\]
Direct verification for \(i=1\) yields \(s_1 = t_1\). For \(i \geq 2\) a routine but tedious expansion (splitting the sums at \(j=i\), expressing the partial sums appearing in \(s_{i-1}\) in terms of \(t_i\), and collecting coefficients) produces the identity
\[
s_i = \rho \, s_{i-1} + \bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i.
\]

Suppose \(A\) is singular. Then there exists a nonzero \(x\) such that \(s_i = 0\) for all \(i = 1, \dots, n\). The recurrence for the \(s_i\) together with \(s_1 = t_1\) immediately implies \(t_1 = 0\). Substituting the vanishing of all \(s_i\) into the recurrence then forces
\[
\bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i = 0, \quad i = 2, \dots, n.
\]
Consequently:
- if \(\rho^2 \neq i/(i-1)\) for a given \(i \in \{2, \dots, n\}\), then necessarily \(t_i = 0\);
- if \(\rho^2 = m/(m-1)\) for some integer \(m \in \{2, \dots, n\}\), then the coefficient of \(t_m\) vanishes and no constraint is imposed on \(t_m\).

The ratios \(m/(m-1)\) for \(m = 2, \dots, n\) are strictly decreasing and lie in \((1, +\infty)\), hence are pairwise distinct. Therefore the only possible positive values of \(\rho\) at which a nontrivial kernel can exist are those satisfying
\[
\rho^2 = \frac{m}{m-1}
\]
for some \(m \in \{2, \dots, n\}\). For each such \(m\) the choice
\[
t_m = c \neq 0, \qquad t_i = 0 \quad \text{for all } i \neq m
\]
is admissible (in particular \(t_1 = 0\)). The corresponding vector \(x\) defined by \(x_i = t_i - \rho t_{i+1}\) (with \(t_{n+1} = 0\)) is nonzero: if \(m = n\) then \(x_n = c\) and \(x_{n-1} = -\rho c\); if \(m < n\) then \(x_{m-1} = -\rho c\). Starting from \(s_1 = t_1 = 0\) and using the recurrence for the \(s_i\), the vanishing of all coefficients \(\bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i\) (which holds because \(t_i = 0\) whenever the coefficient is nonzero, and the coefficient itself vanishes when \(i = m\)) shows by induction that \(s_i = 0\) for every \(i\). Thus each such \(\rho\) indeed produces a nontrivial kernel, so \(A\) is singular.

If \(\rho^2\) equals none of the ratios \(k/(k-1)\) for \(k = 2, \dots, n\), then all \(t_i\) are forced to vanish, which in turn forces \(x = 0\). Hence these are the only positive values of \(\rho\) at which \(A\) can be singular.

The positive values of \(a\) making \(A\) singular are therefore
\[
a_k = \sqrt{\frac{k}{k-1}}, \quad k = 2, 3, \dots, 2026.
\]
Each of these values is realized by the explicit nonzero kernel vector constructed above (with \(m = k\)) and is therefore admissible. The required sum is
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{2026} \sqrt{\frac{k}{k-1}}.
\]

Final answer: \(\sum_{k=2}^{2026} \sqrt{k/(k-1)}\)

content.text:
The matrix \(A\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix with entries
\[
A_{ij} = \min(i,j) \cdot a^{|i-j|},
\]
where \(n = 2026\) and \(a > 0\). The goal is to determine all values of \(a > 0\) for which \(A\) is singular and to compute the sum of these values.

Let \(\rho = a > 0\). For an arbitrary vector \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top\), define the auxiliary quantities
\[
t_i = \sum_{j=i}^n \rho^{j-i} x_j, \quad i = 1, \dots, n
\]
(with the convention \(t_{n+1} = 0\)). These satisfy the backward recurrence
\[
t_i = x_i + \rho \, t_{i+1}, \quad i = 1, \dots, n-1,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
x_i = t_i - \rho \, t_{i+1}, \quad i = 1, \dots, n-1, \qquad x_n = t_n.
\]
Conversely, for any choice of the sequence \((t_1, \dots, t_n)\), the vector \(x\) defined by the preceding formulae produces exactly those \(t_i\).

Denote \(s = A x\), so that the \(i\)-th component is
\[
s_i = \sum_{j=1}^i j \, \rho^{i-j} x_j + i \sum_{j=i+1}^n \rho^{j-i} x_j.
\]
Direct verification for \(i=1\) yields \(s_1 = t_1\). For \(i \geq 2\) a routine but tedious expansion (splitting the sums at \(j=i\), expressing the partial sums appearing in \(s_{i-1}\) in terms of \(t_i\), and collecting coefficients) produces the identity
\[
s_i = \rho \, s_{i-1} + \bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i.
\]

Suppose \(A\) is singular. Then there exists a nonzero \(x\) such that \(s_i = 0\) for all \(i = 1, \dots, n\). The recurrence for the \(s_i\) together with \(s_1 = t_1\) immediately implies \(t_1 = 0\). Substituting the vanishing of all \(s_i\) into the recurrence then forces
\[
\bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i = 0, \quad i = 2, \dots, n.
\]
Consequently:
- if \(\rho^2 \neq i/(i-1)\) for a given \(i \in \{2, \dots, n\}\), then necessarily \(t_i = 0\);
- if \(\rho^2 = m/(m-1)\) for some integer \(m \in \{2, \dots, n\}\), then the coefficient of \(t_m\) vanishes and no constraint is imposed on \(t_m\).

The ratios \(m/(m-1)\) for \(m = 2, \dots, n\) are strictly decreasing and lie in \((1, +\infty)\), hence are pairwise distinct. Therefore the only possible positive values of \(\rho\) at which a nontrivial kernel can exist are those satisfying
\[
\rho^2 = \frac{m}{m-1}
\]
for some \(m \in \{2, \dots, n\}\). For each such \(m\) the choice
\[
t_m = c \neq 0, \qquad t_i = 0 \quad \text{for all } i \neq m
\]
is admissible (in particular \(t_1 = 0\)). The corresponding vector \(x\) defined by \(x_i = t_i - \rho t_{i+1}\) (with \(t_{n+1} = 0\)) is nonzero: if \(m = n\) then \(x_n = c\) and \(x_{n-1} = -\rho c\); if \(m < n\) then \(x_{m-1} = -\rho c\). Starting from \(s_1 = t_1 = 0\) and using the recurrence for the \(s_i\), the vanishing of all coefficients \(\bigl(i - (i-1)\rho^2\bigr) t_i\) (which holds because \(t_i = 0\) whenever the coefficient is nonzero, and the coefficient itself vanishes when \(i = m\)) shows by induction that \(s_i = 0\) for every \(i\). Thus each such \(\rho\) indeed produces a nontrivial kernel, so \(A\) is singular.

If \(\rho^2\) equals none of the ratios \(k/(k-1)\) for \(k = 2, \dots, n\), then all \(t_i\) are forced to vanish, which in turn forces \(x = 0\). Hence these are the only positive values of \(\rho\) at which \(A\) can be singular.

The positive values of \(a\) making \(A\) singular are therefore
\[
a_k = \sqrt{\frac{k}{k-1}}, \quad k = 2, 3, \dots, 2026.
\]
Each of these values is realized by the explicit nonzero kernel vector constructed above (with \(m = k\)) and is therefore admissible. The required sum is
\[
\sum_{k=2}^{2026} \sqrt{\frac{k}{k-1}}.
\]

Final answer: \(\sum_{k=2}^{2026} \sqrt{k/(k-1)}\)
